passages.happening:
“Therefore, there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (verse 1). “For in Christ Jesus the law of the Spirit of life set you free from the law of sin and death” (verse 2).

What the law could not do, because human nature was weak, God did. He sent his own Son “in the likeness of sinful man, as an offering for sin” (verse 3), and condemned sin in the flesh, so that the law's just demand might be met in us who live by the Spirit, not by the flesh (verse 4).

Paul sets two ways of life side by side. Those who live by the flesh set their minds on the flesh; those who live by the Spirit set their minds on the Spirit (verse 5). “The mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace” (verse 6). The mind of the flesh is hostile to God and cannot obey his law (verses 7-8).

“You, however, are controlled not by the flesh, but by the Spirit, if the Spirit of God lives in you” (verse 9). If Christ is in you, your body is still mortal because of sin, but your spirit is alive (verse 10). And the Spirit of the one who raised Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
After the cry of 7:24, ‘Who will rescue me?’, comes the answer. ‘No condemnation’ is a law-court word. The verdict has been given, and it is not guilty. ‘Now’ means already, not only on the last day.

The Holy Spirit fills this chapter. In the whole of Romans 1 to 7 the Spirit is named only a handful of times; in chapter 8 he is named again and again. Chapter 7 had a great deal of ‘I’ and no Spirit. Chapter 8 turns to what God's Spirit does.

‘In the likeness of sinful man’ is careful. Jesus was truly human, sharing our weak and mortal flesh, but Paul does not say he was sinful. ‘As an offering for sin’ uses the language of the sin offering in the temple.

‘The flesh’ and ‘the Spirit’ are not body and soul. ‘Flesh’ here means human life turned from God and relying on itself. ‘Spirit’ means God's own Spirit living in a person. The contrast is between two powers, and two directions for the whole person, body and mind.

Verse 9 is plain: every believer has the Spirit. Paul does not divide Christians into those who have the Spirit and those who do not. ‘If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to Christ.’

Verse 11 looks ahead. The Spirit does not only give new life inside. He will one day raise believers' bodies, as he raised Jesus.
passages.ot:
The law named the sin offering, which a person brought ‘for the sin he has committed’ (Leviticus 4:3). Paul says God himself provided it, in his Son.

The promise of the Spirit within comes from the prophets. Ezekiel heard God say, “I will put My Spirit in you and you will live” (Ezekiel 37:14), in the vision of dry bones coming to life. And: “I will put My Spirit within you and cause you to walk in My statutes” (Ezekiel 36:27). That is what Paul says happens: the law's just demand is met by those who walk by the Spirit.
passages.hard: Does ‘no condemnation’ mean believers can live as they like? Paul has already refused that in chapter 6, and he refuses it again here: those who belong to Christ walk ‘according to the Spirit’. But he will not let that turn into fear. ‘No condemnation’ is not a reward for living well. It is God's verdict for those who are in Christ Jesus. A changed life follows from it, as fruit follows from a root. Christians differ on how this verdict and the new life relate, as the book page sets out, but all hear in verse 1 the same good news: those in Christ are not condemned.
passages.asks: ‘There is now no condemnation.’ Ask whether you live as if you are still waiting for the verdict. Then ask where your mind is set: on what your own nature wants, or on what the Spirit wants. Paul says one way is death and the other is life and peace.

passages.happening:
“Therefore, brothers, we have an obligation, but it is not to the flesh, to live according to it” (verse 12). If you live by the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live (verse 13).

“For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (verse 14). “For you did not receive a spirit of slavery that returns you to fear, but you received the Spirit of sonship, by whom we cry” (verse 15): “Abba! Father!” (verse 15).

“The Spirit Himself testifies with our spirit that we are God’s children” (verse 16). If children, then heirs, “heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ” (verse 17), if indeed we suffer with him, so that we may also be glorified with him (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
‘Abba’ is the Aramaic word for father, the word Jesus himself used when he prayed in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36). Greek-speaking believers in Rome kept the Aramaic word, and added the Greek word for father beside it. It was a word of close family trust. Some have said it meant ‘Daddy’, but many scholars now think that goes too far: grown children used it too. It is warm, and it is respectful.

‘Sonship’ is the Greek huiothesia, a legal word for adoption as a son with full rights of inheritance. In Roman law an adopted son became his new father's heir. Paul says believers have been adopted into God's family, and so they inherit with Christ.

In Paul's world the son was the heir, so ‘sons of God’ meant heirs. Paul uses the word for every believer, women and men alike. In the next verse he says ‘children’, and in another letter he says of all who belong to Christ, “There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female” (Galatians 3:28). Every believer is God's child and heir.

The contrast is between slavery and family. A slave obeys out of fear. A child of the house belongs there. The Spirit does not make believers anxious slaves; he teaches them to call God Father.

‘If indeed we suffer with Him’. Being God's heir does not mean an easy road now. Jesus came to glory by suffering, and his brothers and sisters share his road.
passages.ot:
Israel was called God's son long before. God told Pharaoh, “Israel is My firstborn son” (Exodus 4:22), and Hosea says, “When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called My son” (Hosea 11:1). The ‘adoption as sons’ belonged first to Israel (9:4). Paul says it now reaches all who are led by God's Spirit.

The Psalms describe God as a father: “As a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD has compassion on those who fear Him” (Psalm 103:13).

‘A spirit of slavery that returns you to fear’ may recall Israel in the wilderness, who more than once wanted to go back to Egypt (Numbers 14:3-4).
passages.hard: What if ‘Father’ is a hard word for you? Some readers had a father who was absent, or who hurt them. If your own father was not there, or did not show you love, this verse is not asking you to picture him. It is telling you what you should have been shown, and what God is. God's love as a Father is not limited by the father you had. A psalm says, “Though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will receive me” (Psalm 27:10). If what happened to you still weighs on you, please talk with someone you trust, a pastor, a friend or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul says believers do not have to live in fear like slaves. Ask what fear still drives your relationship with God. Then try praying with the word Jesus used, ‘Father’, and see what changes. Ask what it means for you to be an heir with Christ, and what it may cost to share his road.

passages.t: Creation groans, and the Spirit helps
passages.happening:
“I consider that our present sufferings are not comparable to the glory that will be revealed in us” (verse 18).

“The creation waits in eager expectation for the revelation of the sons of God” (verse 19). It was subjected to futility, not by its own choice, but by the one who subjected it, in hope (verse 20) “that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to decay and brought into the glorious freedom of the children of God” (verse 21).

“We know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until the present time” (verse 22). We ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan too, as we wait for our adoption, “the redemption of our bodies” (verse 23). We were saved in this hope, and hope that is seen is not hope (verse 24). So we wait for it patiently (verse 25).

“In the same way, the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know how we ought to pray, but the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groans too deep for words” (verse 26). And God, who searches hearts, knows the mind of the Spirit, who prays for the saints as God wills (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
Three groans run through this passage: creation groans (verse 22), believers groan (verse 23), and the Spirit groans (verse 26). The world is not as it should be, and Paul does not pretend that it is.

‘The pains of childbirth’ is a picture of hope. A woman in labour is in real pain, but the pain leads to new life. The world's groaning is not the death rattle of a dying world. It is the labour before a birth.

‘Futility’ means frustration, being unable to reach the purpose something was made for. ‘Bondage to decay’ means everything wearing out and dying. Paul says this will not last. Creation will share in the freedom of God's children.

‘Firstfruits’ was the first part of the harvest, offered to God as a sign that the rest was coming. The Spirit in believers now is the first share of the full harvest to come.

‘The redemption of our bodies’. Paul's hope is not escape from the body into a spirit world. It is the resurrection: bodies raised and made new, in a world made new.

Then a word for anyone who cannot pray. ‘We do not know how we ought to pray.’ Paul admits it. The Spirit prays for us, with groans deeper than words. When a believer can only sigh, the sigh is heard.
passages.ot:
Creation's frustration goes back to Eden. After Adam's sin God said, “cursed is the ground because of you” (Genesis 3:17), and “Both thorns and thistles it will yield for you” (Genesis 3:18).

The prophets promised a world made new: “For behold, I will create new heavens and a new earth” (Isaiah 65:17). Isaiah saw a day when “The wolf will live with the lamb” (Isaiah 11:6), and “They will neither harm nor destroy on all My holy mountain” (Isaiah 11:9).

Groaning that God hears is in the exodus story: “So God heard their groaning, and He remembered His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” (Exodus 2:24).
passages.hard:
Who ‘subjected’ creation to futility, and what does Paul hope for it? Most readers say it was God, after Adam's sin, as Genesis 3:17 tells, because only God could subject it ‘in hope’. Paul's hope is not that God will throw the world away and take souls to heaven, but that he will set creation itself free. John Wesley, in a sermon of the early 1780s called ‘The General Deliverance’, took these verses to mean that even the animals will share in the restoration. Christians differ on the details.

These verses are about God's promise for his whole creation. They are not a programme for any party or policy, and these notes do not use them as one. Christians draw from them a call to care for what God made and will renew, and they apply it in different ways.
passages.asks: Paul says the sufferings of now are not worth comparing with the glory to come. Ask what you are groaning under, and whether you think it is the last word. Then think of the times you did not know how to pray. Paul says the Spirit was praying for you. Ask what it would mean to bring God even a wordless sigh.

passages.happening:
“And we know that God works all things together for the good of those who love Him, who are called according to His purpose” (verse 28).

“For those God foreknew, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son, so that He would be the firstborn among many brothers” (verse 29).

“And those He predestined, He also called; those He called, He also justified; those He justified, He also glorified” (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
Verse 28 follows straight on from the groaning of creation, the waiting of believers and the Spirit's prayers. The ‘all things’ Paul has in mind include those sufferings.

Old manuscripts differ slightly here. Some name God as the one who works; others do not, so that the words can be read ‘all things work together’. Translations differ; the BSB has ‘God works’. Either way, Paul means God's purpose at work.

‘The good’ is defined in the next verse: ‘to be conformed to the image of His Son’. God's good for his people is that they become like Jesus. That is more than comfort or success.

‘Firstborn among many brothers’ means that Jesus is the eldest in a large family. In chapter 1 people exchanged the glory of God for images (1:23). Here God restores his image in people, by making them like his Son.

Verse 30 is a chain of five links: foreknew, predestined, called, justified, glorified. ‘Glorified’ is in the past tense, though the glory is still to come (verse 18). Paul speaks of it as if already done, because to God it is as sure as if it were.
passages.ot:
The idea of God's purpose working through evil and suffering is old. Joseph said to the brothers who had sold him: “what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good” (Genesis 50:20).

The image of God goes back to creation: “So God created man in His own image” (Genesis 1:27). Paul says believers are being made into the image of the Son, the true image of God.

God's knowing and choosing before birth appears in Jeremiah's call: “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you” (Jeremiah 1:5).
passages.hard:
Romans 8:28 is a much-loved verse, and an often misused one. It does not call evil good. The ‘all things’ include the suffering, famine and sword of this chapter, and Paul does not say they are good. He says they cannot defeat God's purpose, and he defines the good as being made like Christ. So it is never a line to hand to someone in fresh grief. And it is never a reason to tell someone who has been hurt that the harm was really good for them. If someone has hurt you, what they did was wrong. If you are still in danger, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

Verses 29 and 30 raise an old question. Reformed Christians read ‘foreknew’ as God's loving choice of particular people beforehand, and see in the unbroken chain God's sure work of saving those he chose. Arminian and Wesleyan Christians read ‘foreknew’ as God knowing beforehand who would freely trust him, and see the chain as God's purpose for those who believe. Others read it of a people: God chose a people in Christ, and each person comes into that chosen people by faith. These notes do not choose. All agree that salvation begins with God and ends in glory. The site's Honest Answer, ‘Does God choose us, or do we choose him?’, sets out the case on each side.
passages.asks: Paul says God's good for you is that you become like Jesus. Ask whether that is the good you want, or whether you hoped for something easier. Then look at the chain in verse 30. Ask what it means for you that the one who began this work in you means to finish it.

passages.happening:
“What then shall we say in response to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us?” (verse 31). He did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all. How will he not also, with him, freely give us all things (verse 32)?

“Who will bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies” (verse 33). Who is there to condemn? Christ Jesus, who died and was raised, is at God's right hand, and he is praying for us (verse 34).

“Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall trouble or distress or persecution or famine or nakedness or danger or sword?” (verse 35). As Scripture says, for God's sake his people face death all day long, like sheep for the slaughter (verse 36).

“No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through Him who loved us” (verse 37). “For I am convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither the present nor the future, nor any powers” (verse 38), “neither height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (verse 39).
passages.hearers:
The chapter ends in a courtroom, and the court has nothing left to say. Who can bring a charge? The judge himself has declared his people in the right. Who can condemn? The one who could, Christ, is instead speaking for them.

Paul's list in verse 35 was not imaginary. Paul himself had known hunger, cold, danger and beatings (2 Corinthians 11:23-27). Within a few years of this letter, believers in Rome would face the sword under Nero. The promise is not that these things will not come. It is that they cannot cut believers off from Christ's love.

‘More than conquerors’ is one Greek word, something like ‘super-conquerors’. They do not only survive; they win, not by their own strength but ‘through Him who loved us’.

The list in verses 38 and 39 sweeps through everything: death and life, spiritual powers, time present and to come, the heights and the depths. The ‘principalities’ and ‘powers’ were spiritual forces people feared. Nothing in all creation, Paul says, can come between believers and God's love.
passages.ot:
Verse 32, ‘did not spare His own Son’, reminds many readers of Abraham and Isaac: “you have not withheld your only son from me” (Genesis 22:12). Abraham was spared from giving his son. God did not spare his.

Verses 33 and 34 echo the servant in Isaiah, who says, “The One who vindicates Me is near” and “Who is there to condemn Me?” (Isaiah 50:8-9). Christ at God's right hand recalls Psalm 110: “Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet” (Psalm 110:1).

Verse 36 quotes Psalm 44: “Yet for Your sake we face death all day long; we are considered as sheep to be slaughtered” (Psalm 44:22). In that psalm, Israel complains that it suffers even though it has stayed faithful: “though we have not forgotten You or betrayed Your covenant” (Psalm 44:17). Paul says that suffering for God's sake is not a sign that his love has failed.
passages.hard:
Can a true believer fall away from God's love? Churches answer in different ways. Much of the Reformed and Baptist world holds that those truly saved are kept by God and cannot finally be lost, and they hear that promise here and in John 10:28. Much of the Wesleyan, Arminian and Catholic world holds that a person can turn away and forfeit salvation; they note that Paul's list names forces outside us, and they point to warnings such as Hebrews 6:4-6. These notes do not choose. Both, rightly held, lead to the same place: a humble clinging to Christ, not careless presumption and not gnawing fear. The site's Honest Answer, ‘Can you lose your salvation?’, sets out both.

If you are afraid that you have lost God's love, read verses 38 and 39 slowly. That fear is not usually the mark of someone who has fallen away. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Read Paul's list in verse 35 and add your own: the thing you fear most. Then read verses 38 and 39 aloud. Ask whether you believe that nothing in all creation can separate you from God's love in Christ. If you do, ask what you would stop being afraid of.
